newsitem.title: USA: Latest U.S. tax package would end key tax loopholes.
newsitem.headline: Latest U.S. tax package would end key tax loopholes.

text.p: After tedious negotiation over the biggest tax changes in 16 years, congressional leaders and the White House have agreed on a plan that closes some of Wall Street's favourite tax loopholes to help fund huge tax cuts over the next five years.

The sweeping reform, which aims to cut taxes by $94 billion over the next five years, would restrict tax relief to companies when they use the popular technique in mergers and acquisitions of forming so-called "Morris Trusts," according to a senior congressional aide.

The Clinton administration and lawmakers contend that companies have exploited tax relief, intended only for internal corporate restructurings, by using these special trusts in mergers and acquisitions.

Using a Morris Trust, corporations have been allowed to spin off tax-free to their shareholders units of companies they acquire. The latest proposal would only allow such tax-free treatment for internal restructuring, a measure that appeared in an earlier Senate version.

For example, AirTouch Communications Inc.'s $5 billion purchase of the wireless business of U S West Inc.'s US West Media Group would be taxable under the provision, a senior congressional aide said Tuesday.
A spokeswoman for AirTouch said it may need to renegotiate the deal if it were taxable.

San Francisco-based AirTouch announced the $5 billion purchase in April shortly after Congress proposed the bill that would eliminate Morris Trust tax-free provisions for certain spin-offs by publicly traded companies.

The deal, which would create the nation's second largest cellular phone company behind giant AT&T Corp., had the same strategic objective of an earlier pact in 1994, but was conditioned upon getting tax relief by using "Morris Trust" tax-free provisions.
AirTouch would prefer to be grandfathered in under the Morris Trust, but the spokeswoman said the company is prepared to move ahead with the deal.
"We said if we were not able to be grandfathered under the 'Morris Trust,' we can revert back to the 1994 deal or choose to renegotiate with U S West," the spokeswoman said.

Taking aim at another loophole, the tax reform plan blocks investors from deferring their capital gains when they sell their stock holdings short, a technique known as "shorting against the box," according to a senior congressional aide.
These transactions allow investors to reap their profits, but put off any capital gains taxes. This is done by borrowing and then selling the same security to help lock in a future price on holdings.
Under the latest proposal, gains and losses would have to be recorded at the time of the transaction.

While lawmakers are eager to end this practice, they disagree over whether the tax change should be retroactive, a plan that has Wall Street on edge. But the latest proposal would apply mostly to future transactions, one tax lawyer familiar with the package said.
Despite the loophole closures, the latest package offers some tax relief to companies, mainly from the corporate alternative minimum tax, a special levy to ensure companies pay at least some taxes.

Under the latest proposal, many small businesses would be exempt from the tax. In addition, firms could more easily depreciate capital expenditures without facing an alternative minimum tax liability. The alternative minimum tax relief is expected to cost the federal government $6.8 billion over five years.

The tax bill did not include a capital gains tax cut for corporations, a provision that was dropped in the earlier unified House-Senate Republican tax plan. But the individual capital gains rate would be reduced to a top rate of 20 percent from 28 percent. This would be reduced to 18 percent for investors holding assets for at least five years.
